title: Saving every version
objectives: See what problem version control solves
Use the history to narrow down where a bug arrived

screens.title: Saving every version
screens.prose: A script that worked on Monday gives nonsense on Thursday. Something changed in between, but what? We will see how to keep every version, so the question has an answer.
On Monday your returns script printed an average daily return of 0.04%. Today it prints −3.10%, which cannot be right. You have been keeping copies by hand.
screens.question: Which file holds Monday's working code?

options.why: You trusted the name. It was last saved on Tuesday, so it may already hold Tuesday's edits.
You trusted the word final. It was saved on Wednesday, two days after Monday, and later files followed it.
You read fixed as working. It was saved on Thursday, after the result broke, so it holds today's attempt.

options.text: None of them for certain: no file was last saved on Monday

hints.text: Look at the Last saved column. Which day do you need?
Every date in this column is later than Monday.
Each file was saved again after Monday, so Monday's contents were overwritten in every one.

feedback.correct: No file still holds Monday's version. Every one was saved again later.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the dates rather than the names.

explain.text: You checked the dates, not the names. Each save replaced what the file held before, so Monday's code is gone. Copies made by hand keep some versions, but rarely the one you need.

screens.prose: Now suppose that, six times over the week, you froze a copy of the whole project: a **snapshot**. Later you run the script on each snapshot. The chart shows what each one prints.

state.caption: Average daily return from each snapshot, in %

screens.question: Tap the first snapshot that gives the broken result.

hints.text: Which results look sensible, and which look broken?
These two snapshots give −3.10%.
Snapshots 1 to 4 give about 0.05%. Snapshot 5 is the first to give −3.10%.

feedback.correct: Snapshot 5 is the first broken one.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the earliest snapshot whose result is −3.10%.

byKey.m6: Snapshot 6 is broken, but so is 5, which came earlier. The bug arrived at the first broken one.
byKey.m4: Snapshot 4 still gives 0.05%, a sensible result. The break comes one snapshot later.
byKey.m1: Snapshot 1 gives 0.04%, the Monday result. The break comes much later.

explain.text: You found the first broken snapshot, number 5. So the bug is in whatever changed between snapshots 4 and 5. Instead of a whole project to search, you have one stretch of edits.

screens.prose: A snapshot saved by **Git** is called a **commit**. Git keeps your commits in order, each one pointing back to the one before. Here are your six, oldest on the left.

params.label: A chain of commits, each pointing back to the one before

state.caption: Commit 5 is the first to give the broken result

screens.question: Which two commits should you compare to find the bug?

options.why: You compared with the first commit. That mixes in every change since Monday, and most of them are harmless.
Both of these are broken. Comparing them shows only changes made after the bug arrived.

options.text: Commit 6 alone, read from top to bottom
options.why: Reading the newest commit means searching every line. Comparing two commits shows only the lines that changed.

hints.text: Where does the result go from fine to broken?
These two sit either side of the break.
4 is the last good commit and 5 the first broken one. Their differences contain the bug.

feedback.correct: The last good commit and the first broken one.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pick the pair either side of the break.

explain.text: Commit 4 works and commit 5 does not, so the bug is among the changes between them. That might be three lines out of three hundred. This is the main reason to keep commits.

screens.prose: Commit 5 was made on Wednesday at 17:52, by you, with the message "Use close-to-close returns". Think about what Git must keep to rebuild the project as it was then.

params.label: A chain of commits, each pointing back to the one before

screens.question: What does a commit record? Select all that apply.

options.text: Every file of the project, as it was at that moment
The result the script printed when you ran it
options.why: Git stores files, not what running them printed. A result is in a commit only if you saved it to a file and committed that file.

options.text: Every save you made since the commit before
options.why: Git does not watch your saves. It copies the files once, at the moment you commit.

hints.text: What would you need to rebuild the project exactly as it was?
This is the commit the prose describes.
The files, the message, the author and the time are all recorded. Git never sees your saves or your script's output.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Git records the files and facts about the commit, nothing it did not see.

byKey.output: You picked the script's output. Git never runs your code; it stores the files.
byKey.saves: You picked every save. Git only sees the files at the moment you commit.

explain.text: A commit holds the whole project plus three facts: the message, the author and the time. It also records which commit came before it. That link is what makes the commits a chain.

screens.prose: Commit 5 changed only `returns.py`. The project also has `plot.py`, which was last changed in commit 3.

params.label: A chain of commits, each pointing back to the one before

screens.question: Does commit 5 contain `plot.py`?

options.text: Yes, the same `plot.py` as in commit 4

options.why: You treated a commit as a list of changes. A commit is the whole project, and unchanged files come along as they were.
You looked for `plot.py` where it last changed. Every later commit carries it too, unchanged.

hints.text: If you asked Git for the project as it was at commit 5, would the chart code be missing?
plot.py changed here and nowhere later.
A commit is a snapshot of every file. plot.py was not edited after commit 3, so commits 4, 5 and 6 hold that same version.

feedback.correct: Every commit is the whole project. Unchanged files are carried along.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A commit is a snapshot of every file, not only the ones you changed.

explain.text: Each commit is a complete snapshot, so commit 5 contains `plot.py` exactly as commit 3 left it. Git avoids storing a second identical copy, but that is invisible to you. Any commit can rebuild the whole project.

screens.prose: A different project. You ran the backtest on commit 2: fine. On commit 6 it is broken. You never ran it on 3, 4 or 5.

params.label: A chain of commits, each pointing back to the one before

state.caption: ✓ ran fine, ✗ broken, no mark: never run

screens.question: Tap every commit that could be the one that brought in the bug.

hints.text: Which commits came after the last one known to work?
These two you have checked.
Commit 2 was fine, so the bug arrived later: in 3, 4, 5 or 6. Commit 6 itself is a suspect too.

feedback.correct: Any of 3, 4, 5 or 6 could hold it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep every commit after the last good one, up to and including the broken one.

byKey.not-six: You left out commit 6. It is broken, so the bug may have arrived in 6 itself.
byKey.only-six: You blamed the commit where you noticed the problem. It may have been there since 3, 4 or 5.
byKey.c1: Commit 1 came before commit 2, which worked. The bug cannot be there.
byKey.c2: You ran commit 2 and it was fine. The bug arrived later.

explain.text: You kept everything after the last good commit, including the broken one itself. Running the backtest on commit 4 next would split the suspects in two. That is how a long history is searched quickly.

screens.prose: You use Git now. This morning you committed once, then kept editing and saving. The 12:40 version is broken, and the 11:30 version was fine.
screens.question: Which earlier versions of `returns.py` can Git give you back?

options.why: You assumed Git keeps every save. It records files only when you commit, so the 10:15 and 11:30 versions are gone.

options.text: The 11:30 version, the last good one
options.why: You expected Git to have watched your saves. It never saw 11:30, because you did not commit then.

options.text: None, because the file has changed since
options.why: A commit stays in the history whatever you do to the file later. The 09:00 version is safe.

hints.text: Which row is a commit, and which rows are only saves?
Only this row added a snapshot to the history.
Saving writes over the file. Git copied it only at 09:00.

feedback.correct: Only the commit is in the history. The saves overwrote each other.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which moments Git actually recorded.

byKey.all: You took every save as a snapshot. Only `git commit` adds one; saving writes over the file.
byKey.last: You expected Git to have kept the 11:30 save. It never saw it, because there was no commit then.

explain.text: Saving overwrites the file; only a commit adds a snapshot. The good 11:30 version was never committed, so it is lost. Commit whenever the project is in a state you might want back.

screens.prose: Here is what you have been using. A **commit** is a snapshot of the whole project, with a message, an author and a time. Each commit points back to the one before, so the commits form a chain: the **history**. Git is a **version control** system: it keeps that history for you.
screens.question: Which of these adds a new snapshot to the history?

options.text: Saving the file in your editor
options.why: Saving overwrites the file; the history does not change. You saw the 11:30 save vanish.
Running reads the files and changes nothing in the history.

hints.text: On the morning you just looked at, which moment could Git give back?
Only the 09:00 commit was recorded. The saves were not.

feedback.correct: Only a commit adds a snapshot.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think back to the morning of saves.

explain.text: You saw that only the 09:00 commit survived. Saves and runs leave the history untouched. Git records what you commit, when you commit it.

screens.prose: Your moving-average backtest on SPY now reports a Sharpe ratio of 2.91. For a rule this simple, that is too good to be true. Each commit is named by a short code, its **hash**.

rows: Trade on the same day's close

state.caption: Oldest commit at the top. Each Sharpe ratio is from running the backtest on that commit.

screens.question: Tap the hash of the commit whose changes you would read first.

hints.text: Where does the Sharpe ratio jump?
Read down this column.
It goes from 0.48 at 71ad3be to 2.91 at e52f9c1. The commit after the jump is the one to read.

feedback.correct: The Sharpe ratio jumped from 0.48 to 2.91 at e52f9c1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the commit where the Sharpe ratio jumps.

byKey.r5c0: You picked the newest commit. It only plotted the curve; the Sharpe ratio was already 2.91 before it.
byKey.r4c0: This commit only labelled the chart. The jump happened one commit earlier.
byKey.r2c0: Charging costs lowered the Sharpe ratio from 0.62 to 0.48. That is what costs should do.
byKey.r1c0: The signal gave a believable 0.62. The jump came two commits later.

explain.text: The jump to 2.91 arrived with e52f9c1, so its changes are the suspects. Trading on the same day's close uses a price the strategy could not have known in time: lookahead. The history pointed you to one commit instead of the whole project.

ideas: Saving a file overwrites it. Only a commit adds a snapshot to the history.
A commit is the whole project, with a message, an author, a time and a link to the commit before.
The bug is in the changes between the last good commit and the first broken one.

formula.name: Finding where a bug arrived
formula.note: Compare these two. Their differences hold the bug.

summary.trap: Git does not keep your saves. A version you never committed cannot be brought back.

quiz.prose: You commit, then save `returns.py` five times, then commit again.
quiz.question: How many snapshots of the project does the history now hold?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count only the commits.

byKey.all: You counted the saves as snapshots too. Only the two commits were recorded.
byKey.saves: You counted the saves. Git never sees them; it records only commits.
byKey.six: You counted the saves and one commit. Saves add nothing; both commits count.

explain.text: Each commit adds one snapshot; saving the file adds none. So the history holds 2. The four saves in between are lost unless the last one is committed.

quiz.prose: Commit 7 gives the right result. Commit 8, the next one, gives a wrong result.
quiz.question: Where is the bug?

options.text: Among the changes commit 8 made to commit 7
In commit 1, where the project started
options.why: You went back to the start. Commit 7 works, so everything up to 7 is fine.

options.text: In commit 7, the one before the break
options.why: Commit 7 gives the right result, so its code is fine. The bug came in with 8.
You ignored that commit 7 works. That rules out everything before 8.

feedback.correct: Commit 7 works and 8 does not, so 8's changes hold the bug.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use the last commit that works.

explain.text: Commit 7 is good and commit 8 is bad. The only thing between them is what commit 8 changed. Comparing the two shows exactly those lines.

quiz.prose: Commit 12 changed only `signal.py`. You ask Git for the project as it was at commit 12.
quiz.question: Which files do you get?

options.text: Every file of the project, as it was at commit 12

options.why: You treated a commit as just its changes. It is a snapshot of the whole project.
A commit does not depend on what its neighbours changed. It holds every file.

feedback.correct: A commit rebuilds the whole project.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A commit is a snapshot of every file.

explain.text: Each commit is complete. Files that commit 12 did not touch come back exactly as they were then. That is why any commit can be run on its own.

quiz.prose: Your backtest gave a Sharpe ratio of 0.8 on commit 3. Run again on commit 4, it gives 1.6. Commit 4 changed only `README.md`, the project's description. The script reads `prices.csv`, which is not in any commit.
quiz.question: What should you suspect first?

options.why: You blamed the only change in the commit. A description is never run, so it cannot move a result.
Commit 3 gave a sensible 0.8. And the code did not change between 3 and 4.
Git rebuilds files exactly. The difference lies outside what Git keeps.

feedback.correct: The code did not change, so look at what Git does not keep.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what can change outside the commits.

explain.text: The code in commits 3 and 4 is identical, yet the result moved. So something outside the history changed: here, the data file. The history only explains what is in it.
